summary: Provides source code for the US Secure Hash Algorithms, including SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384 and SHA-512, and HMAC-SHA, to make them conveniently available. It is informational and has been replaced by RFC 6234.

eli5.summary: Hash functions turn any file into a short fingerprint. This gives programmers sample code for them.

subtitle: Reference implementations of the US SHA hash functions in C code.

tldr.problem: Developers needed reliable source code for the newer SHA algorithms (SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, SHA-512) that the US government standardized, plus implementations of HMAC-SHA keyed authentication codes.
tldr.mechanism: This RFC provides complete C source code for all SHA variants and HMAC-SHA, handling messages of arbitrary bit length, adapted from the US FIPS 180-2 standard.
tldr.outcome: The code became a widely used reference implementation and was later updated and consolidated in RFC 6234.

today: RFC 4634 is an Informational RFC. It was superseded by RFC 6234, which updates the reference implementations and adds support for additional programming languages and related functions like HKDF.

sections.title: Secure Hash Algorithms and Authentication
sections.content:
The United States has standardized a suite of Secure Hash Algorithms (SHAs) for creating compact fingerprints of data. These algorithms are used to detect whether a message or file has been tampered with, and in digital signatures and message authentication. RFC 4634 provides source code implementations for four SHA variants: SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512, plus code for HMAC-SHA, which uses SHA with a secret key to authenticate messages.

The code is adapted from FIPS 180-2, the US Federal Information Processing Standard, and can handle input messages of any bit length. It also updates the SHA-1 code from RFC 3174 to accept arbitrary bit lengths. The code is provided under a royalty-free license for both commercial and non-commercial use.
sections.eli5: A hash is a short code computed from data that changes if anything changes. This document gives programmers working code for several types of hashes that the US government standardized.

sections.title: How SHA Hash Functions Work
sections.content:
Hash functions take input of any length and produce a fixed-length output called a message digest. SHA-224 and SHA-256 produce 224-bit and 256-bit digests respectively; SHA-384 and SHA-512 produce 384-bit and 512-bit digests. The core idea is that it is computationally infeasible to find two different messages that produce the same digest, and infeasible to reverse a digest back to the original message.

The algorithms work on blocks of data. SHA-224 and SHA-256 process 512-bit blocks, while SHA-384 and SHA-512 process 1024-bit blocks. Before hashing, the message is padded with a single 1 bit, followed by zeros, followed by the original message length in binary. This padding ensures the result is a multiple of the block size. The algorithm then applies bitwise operations (AND, OR, XOR, rotations) and addition in a carefully specified sequence to produce the final digest.
sections.eli5: A hash takes any file, no matter how big, and turns it into a fixed-size fingerprint. If anything in the file changes, the fingerprint changes completely.

sections.title: Message Padding and Block Processing
sections.content:
Before hashing, a message is padded to make its length a multiple of 512 bits (for SHA-224/256) or 1024 bits (for SHA-384/512). The padding consists of a 1 bit appended to the message, followed by the minimum number of 0 bits needed, followed by a 64-bit (or 128-bit for the larger variants) representation of the original message's bit length.

For example, if hashing the 40-bit message 0x6162636465 (the text 'abcde' in hex), with SHA-256, the message is padded to: the original bits, then a 1 bit, then 407 zeros, then the 64-bit length field (40 in binary). This produces exactly 512 bits. The padded message is then broken into 512-bit (or 1024-bit) blocks and processed sequentially through the hash algorithm.
sections.eli5: The message gets a marker bit added, then padding, then the length, all to make the total a nice round number the computer likes.

sections.title: SHA Variants and HMAC-SHA Authentication
sections.content:
The RFC specifies four distinct SHA algorithms. SHA-256 uses 32-bit word operations and produces a 256-bit digest, suitable for general-purpose hashing. SHA-224 is a truncated version of SHA-256 producing a 224-bit digest when a shorter fingerprint is acceptable. The 64-bit variants, SHA-384 and SHA-512, operate on 64-bit words and produce 384-bit and 512-bit digests respectively, providing stronger collision resistance for high-security applications.

HMAC-SHA extends the SHA algorithms for message authentication. An HMAC computes a hash using a secret key, so only someone with the key can verify the digest. The code provided supports HMAC with any of the SHA variants and handles arbitrary bit-length messages. HMAC is used to verify both the integrity and authenticity of messages—that they have not been changed and came from someone with the correct key.
sections.eli5: SHA-256 is the most common one; bigger numbers give longer fingerprints. HMAC-SHA adds a secret key so only authorized people can verify the fingerprint.

sections.title: The Provided C Code
sections.content:
RFC 4634 includes complete C source code for SHA-1, SHA-224, SHA-256, SHA-384, and SHA-512, plus HMAC implementations. The code is organized into a header file defining the data structures and function prototypes, separate C files for each algorithm's core logic, a unified interface file that handles different SHA variants, and a test driver that validates the implementations against known test vectors.

The code is released under a simple license permitting any use, commercial or non-commercial, provided that derivative works do not contain misleading authorship information and RFC 4634 is referenced in material mentioning the software. The authors provide the code as-is without warranty.
sections.eli5: The document includes ready-to-compile C code for all the hash types, plus a test program to check if the code is working right.

sections.title: Status Today
sections.content: RFC 4634 is an Informational RFC providing reference implementations. It was updated and consolidated in RFC 6234, which added implementations in additional programming languages and further refinements.
sections.eli5: A newer RFC, 6234, improved this one with code in more programming languages.
